{{Short description|Property of rank functions of matroids}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Ingleton's inequality''' is an [[inequality (mathematics)|inequality]] that is satisfied by the [[matroid rank|rank function]] of any [[representable matroid]]. In this sense it is a necessary condition for representability of a [[matroid]] over a [[finite field]].  For a matroid ''M'' and its rank function ''ρ'', Ingleton's inequality states that for any subsets ''X''<sub>1</sub>, ''X''<sub>2</sub>, ''X''<sub>3</sub> and ''X''<sub>4</sub> in the [[support (mathematics)|support]] of ''M'', the inequality

: ''ρ''(''X''<sub>1</sub>) + ''ρ''(''X''<sub>2</sub>) + ''ρ''(''X''<sub>1</sub>∪''X''<sub>2</sub>∪''X''<sub>3</sub>) + ''ρ''(''X''<sub>1</sub>∪''X''<sub>2</sub>∪''X''<sub>4</sub>) + ''ρ''(''X''<sub>3</sub>∪''X''<sub>4</sub>) ≤ ''ρ''(''X''<sub>1</sub>∪''X''<sub>2</sub>) + ''ρ''(''X''<sub>1</sub>∪''X''<sub>3</sub>) + ''ρ''(''X''<sub>1</sub>∪''X''<sub>4</sub>) + ''ρ''(''X''<sub>2</sub>∪''X''<sub>3</sub>) + ''ρ''(''X''<sub>2</sub>∪''X''<sub>4</sub>)
is satisfied.

[[Aubrey William Ingleton]], an English mathematician, wrote an important paper in 1969<ref name=Ing71>{{Cite book | zbl=0222.05025 | last=Ingleton | first=A.W. | chapter=Representation of matroids | pages=149–167 | title=Combinatorial mathematics and its applications. Proceedings, Oxford, 1969 | editor-last=Welsh | editor-first=D.J.A. | year=1971 | publisher=Academic Press | isbn=0-12-743350-3   }}</ref> in which he surveyed the representability problem in matroids.  Although the article is mainly expository, in this paper Ingleton stated and [[mathematical proof|proved]] Ingleton's inequality, which has found interesting applications in [[information theory]], [[matroid|matroid theory]], and [[network coding]].<ref name="Ahlswede2000">{{cite journal| first=Rudolf| last=Ahlswede| authorlink=Rudolf Ahlswede|author2= N. Cai|author3=Shuo-Yen Robert Li|author4=Raymond Wai-Ho Yeung| title=Network Information Flow| journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory| pages= 1204–1216| year= 2000| doi=10.1109/18.850663| volume=46| issue=4}}</ref>

== Importance of inequality ==

There are interesting connections between matroids, the [[Entropic vector|entropy region]] and [[group theory]]. Some of those connections are revealed by Ingleton's Inequality.

Perhaps, the more interesting application of Ingleton's inequality concerns the computation of [[network coding]] capacities.  [[Linear network coding|Linear coding solutions]] are constrained by the inequality and it has an important consequence:

:The region of achievable rates using [[linear network coding]] could be, in some cases, strictly smaller than the region of achievable rates using general network coding.<ref name="Dougherty2005">{{cite journal| first=R.| last= Dougherty|author2=C. Freiling|author2-link=Chris Freiling |author3=K. Zeger | title=Insufficiency of Linear Network Codes| journal=IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory Adelaide, Australia| pages= 264–267| year= 2005}}</ref><ref name="Dougherty2007">{{cite journal| first=R.| last= Dougherty|author2=C. Freiling|author2-link=Chris Freiling |author3=K. Zeger | title=Networks, matroids, and non-Shannon information inequalities| journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory| pages= 1949–1969| year= 2007| volume=53| issue=6| doi=10.1109/TIT.2007.896862| s2cid= 27096| citeseerx=10.1.1.218.3066}}</ref><ref>{{Cite FTP |doi=10.1109/TIT.2002.807285|title=Linear network coding|volume=49|issue=2|pages=371|year=2003|last1=Li|first1=S.-Y.R.|last2=Yeung|first2=R.W.|last3=Ning Cai|server=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory|url-status=dead|url=ftp://doc.nit.ac.ir/cee/m.zahabi/Articles/network%20coding/10[1}}</ref>
 
For definitions, see e.g.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1109/SURV.2013.013013.00104 |title=Network Coding Theory: A Survey |journal=IEEE Communications Surveys & Tutorials |volume=15 |issue=4 |pages=1950 |year=2013 |last1=Bassoli |first1=Riccardo |last2=Marques |first2=Hugo |last3=Rodriguez |first3=Jonathan |last4=Shum |first4=Kenneth W. |last5=Tafazolli |first5=Rahim |s2cid=691027 }}
</ref>

== Proof ==

'''Theorem''' (Ingleton's inequality):<ref>Oxley, James (1992), Matroid Theory, Oxford: Oxford University Press, {{ISBN|0-19-853563-5}}, [[Mathematical Reviews|MR]] [https://www.ams.org/mathscinet-getitem?mr=1207587 1207587], [[Zentralblatt MATH|Zbl]] [http://www.zentralblatt-math.org/zmath/en/search/?format=complete&q=an:0784.05002 0784.05002].</ref> Let ''M'' be a [[linear matroid|representable matroid]] with rank function ''ρ'' and let ''X''<sub>1</sub>, ''X''<sub>2</sub>, ''X''<sub>3</sub> and ''X''<sub>4</sub> be subsets of the support set of ''M'', denoted by the symbol ''E''(''M'').  Then:

: ''ρ''(''X''<sub>1</sub>)+''ρ''(''X''<sub>2</sub>) + ''ρ''(''X''<sub>1</sub>∪''X''<sub>2</sub>∪''X''<sub>3</sub>) + ''ρ''(''X''<sub>1</sub>∪''X''<sub>2</sub>∪''X''<sub>4</sub>) + ''ρ''(''X''<sub>3</sub>∪''X''<sub>4</sub>) ≤ ''ρ''(''X''<sub>1</sub>∪''X''<sub>2</sub>) + ''ρ''(''X''<sub>1</sub>∪''X''<sub>3</sub>) + ''ρ''(''X''<sub>1</sub>∪''X''<sub>4</sub>) + ''ρ''(''X''<sub>2</sub>∪''X''<sub>3</sub>) + ''ρ''(''X''<sub>2</sub>∪''X''<sub>4</sub>).

To prove the inequality we have to show the following result:

'''Proposition''':  Let ''V''<sub>1</sub>,''V''<sub>2</sub>, ''V''<sub>3</sub> and ''V''<sub>4</sub> be [[linear subspace|subspaces]] of a [[vector space]] ''V'', then

# dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>3</sub>) ≥ dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>3</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>)                                 + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>)
# dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>3</sub>∩''V''<sub>4</sub>) ≥ dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>3</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>4</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>)
# dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>3</sub>∩''V''<sub>4</sub>) ≥ dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>3</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>4</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>)
# dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>2</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>3</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>) ≤ dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>2</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>)
   
Where ''V<sub>i</sub>''+''V<sub>j</sub>'' represent the [[direct sum]] of the two subspaces.

'''Proof (proposition)''':  We will use frequently the standard vector space identity:
dim(''U'') + dim(''W'') = dim(''U''+''W'') + dim(''U''∩''W'').

1. It is clear that (''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>) + ''V''<sub>3</sub> ⊆ (''V''<sub>1</sub>+ ''V''<sub>3</sub>) ∩ (''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>), then
{|
|-
| dim((''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>)+''V''<sub>3</sub>) || ≤ || dim((''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>2</sub>)∩(''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>)), || hence
|}
 
{|
|-
| dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>3</sub>) || = ||  dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>3</sub>) − dim((''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>)+''V''<sub>3</sub>)
|-
|  || ≥ || dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>3</sub>) − dim((''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>)∩(''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>))
|-
|  || = || dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>3</sub>) – {dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>)                                              – dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>)}
|-
|  || = || dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>3</sub>) – dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>)
|}

2. It is clear that (''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>3</sub>) + (''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>4</sub>) ⊆ (''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>), then
{|
|-
| dim{(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>3</sub>)+(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>4</sub>)} || ≤ || dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>), || hence
|}

{|
|-
| dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>3</sub>∩''V''<sub>4</sub>) || = || dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>3</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>4</sub>) − dim{(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>3</sub>) + (''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>4</sub>)}
|-
|  || ≥ || dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>3</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>4</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>)
|}

3. From (1) and (2) we have:

{|
|-
| dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>3</sub>∩''V''<sub>4</sub>) || ≥ || dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>3</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>4</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>)
|-
|  || ≥ || dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>3</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>4</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>)
|-
|  || = || dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>3</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>4</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>)
|}
 
4.  From (3) we have

{|
|-
| dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>) || ≤ || dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>3</sub>∩''V''<sub>4</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>3</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>4</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>)+ dim(''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>)
|}
 
If we add (dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>)+dim(''V''<sub>2</sub>)+dim(''V''<sub>3</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>)) at both sides  of the last inequality, we get

{|
|-
| dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>2</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>3</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>) ||  ≤  || dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>3</sub>∩''V''<sub>4</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+dim(''V''<sub>2</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>3</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>3</sub>) − dim(''V''<sub>4</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>3</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>) + dim(''V''<sub>2</sub>+''V''<sub>4</sub>)
|}
                                          
Since the inequality dim(''V''<sub>1</sub>∩''V''<sub>2</sub>∩''V''<sub>3</sub>∩''V''<sub>4</sub>) ≤  dim(''V''<sub>3</sub>∩''V''<sub>4</sub>) holds, we have finished the proof.♣

'''Proof (Ingleton's inequality)''':  Suppose that ''M'' is a representable matroid and let ''A'' = [''v''<sub>1</sub> ''v''<sub>2</sub> … ''v''<sub>''n''</sub>] be a [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] such that ''M'' = ''M''(''A'').
For  ''X'', ''Y'' ⊆ E(''M'') = {1,2, …, ''n''}, define ''U'' = <{''V<sub>i</sub>'' : ''i'' ∈ ''X''&thinsp;}>, as the [[linear span|span]] of the vectors in ''V<sub>i</sub>'', and we define ''W'' = <{''V<sub>j</sub>'' : ''j''  ∈ ''Y''&thinsp;}> accordingly.

If we suppose that ''U'' = <{''u''<sub>1</sub>, ''u''<sub>2</sub>, … ,''u''<sub>''m''</sub>}> and ''W'' = <{''w''<sub>1</sub>, ''w''<sub>2</sub>, … ,''w''<sub>''r''</sub>}> then clearly we have <{''u''<sub>1</sub>, ''u''<sub>2</sub>, …, ''u''<sub>''m''</sub>, ''w''<sub>1</sub>, ''w''<sub>2</sub>, …, ''w''<sub>''r''</sub>}> = ''U'' + ''W''.

Hence:
''r''(''X''∪''Y'') = dim&thinsp;<{''v<sub>i</sub>'' : ''i''  ∈ ''X''&thinsp;} ∪ {''v<sub>j</sub>'' : ''j''  ∈ ''Y''&thinsp;}> = dim(''V'' + ''W''&thinsp;).

Finally, if we define ''V<sub>i</sub>'' = {''v<sub>r</sub>'' : ''r'' ∈ ''X<sub>i</sub>''&thinsp;} for ''i'' = 1,2,3,4, then by last inequality and the item (4) of the above proposition, we get the result.
